answer: Budget impact analysis (BIA) estimates the financial consequences of adopting a new intervention within a specific budget context. Unlike cost-effectiveness analysis, which measures health gained per dollar, BIA asks whether the total spending change is affordable, when costs are incurred across years, and how scale interacts with a fixed budget limit. A program can be highly cost-effective per QALY yet still exceed available funds, so cost-effectiveness and affordability are independent considerations that a payer must weigh together when allocating a constrained budget.

faqs.q: What is the difference between budget impact analysis and cost-effectiveness analysis?
faqs.a: Cost-effectiveness analysis measures health gained per dollar spent, while budget impact analysis measures the total change in spending against a fixed budget. A program can be cost-effective per QALY yet unaffordable at scale.

faqs.q: Can a cost-effective program still be unaffordable?
faqs.a: Yes. A program may deliver a low cost per QALY and still exceed the available budget once it is scaled to serve a large population, because cost-effectiveness and affordability are independent.

faqs.q: Why does the timing of costs matter in a budget impact analysis?
faqs.a: Budget impact analysis accounts for when costs fall, such as Year 1 versus Year 5, because a payer must fund the cash outlay within each budget cycle rather than only over the program's full horizon.
